summary: This document registers status codes that let a mail server tell a sender that a message was rejected or deferred because of email authentication failures. It updates RFC 7208, since some registered codes replace those it recommended.

eli5.summary: When a post office refuses a letter, it helps to say why. This RFC gives mail servers standard codes to say a message failed checks that prove who sent it.

subtitle: New SMTP status codes that tell a sender its message was refused because it failed email authentication checks.

tldr.problem: Mail servers often reject or defer messages because of DKIM, SPF or reverse DNS checks, but the existing enhanced status codes had no way to say so.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7372 registers seven new enhanced status codes, X.7.20 to X.7.26, each tied to a specific kind of authentication failure and usually paired with basic code 550.
tldr.outcome: Senders and software such as mailing list managers can tell authentication failures apart from bad addresses. The RFC updates RFC 7208, because some of its codes replace those recommended there.

today: RFC 7372 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 7208, since some of its codes replace the ones that document recommended.

sections.title: Why New Status Codes
sections.content:
RFC 3463 introduced Enhanced Mail System Status Codes, and RFC 5248 created an IANA registry for them. RFC 6376 and RFC 7208 defined two message authentication protocols: DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) and the Sender Policy Framework (SPF). A third common acceptance test is the reverse DNS check on a client's IP address, described in Section 3 of RFC 7001.

The existing enhanced status codes had nothing to say that a message was refused or deferred because of local policy about any of these mechanisms. That information is useful to agents that need more than basic handling information about why a message was rejected on receipt. This document introduces enhanced status codes for those cases.
sections.eli5: Mail servers could already say 'no', but not 'no, because I could not check who really sent this'. This RFC adds those words.

sections.title: DKIM Failure Codes
sections.content:
Three codes cover DKIM, and they rely on two definitions. A signature is passing if the basic DKIM verification algorithm from RFC 6376 succeeds. It is acceptable if it also meets any locally defined requirements, for example that certain header fields are signed or that there are no partial signatures.

  • X.7.20, 'No passing DKIM signature found': the message had no passing DKIM signatures.
  • X.7.21, 'No acceptable DKIM signature found': there were passing signatures, but none were acceptable.
  • X.7.22, 'No valid author-matched DKIM signature found': there were passing signatures, but none had an identifier matching the author address in the From header field. This is a special case of X.7.21.

Each is paired with basic status code 550, and each description notes that using it violates the advice of Section 6.1 of RFC 6376.
sections.eli5: A signature is like a wax seal on a letter. These codes say 'there was no good seal', 'the seal was real but not one I accept', or 'the seal did not match the name of the person who wrote the letter'.

sections.title: SPF, Reverse DNS and Multiple Failure Codes
sections.content:
Two codes cover SPF. X.7.23, 'SPF validation failed', is returned when an SPF check produced a 'fail' result contrary to local policy, and is used in place of 5.7.1 as described in Section 8.4 of RFC 7208. X.7.24, 'SPF validation error', is returned when evaluating SPF resulted in an error. It is used in place of 4.4.3 or 5.5.2, as described in Sections 8.6 and 8.7 of RFC 7208, and its associated basic status code is 451/550.

X.7.25, 'Reverse DNS validation failed', is returned when an SMTP client's IP address failed a reverse DNS check, contrary to local policy. X.7.26, 'Multiple authentication checks failed', is returned when a message failed more than one authentication check. It does not say which mechanisms failed.

All of these registrations name M. Kucherawy as submitter and the IESG as change controller.
sections.eli5: Other codes say 'the sender's mail was not sent from a place its domain approves', 'something went wrong while I was checking', 'the sending computer's address did not look right', or 'several checks failed at once'.

sections.title: Using the Codes in Practice
sections.content:
SMTP lets only one enhanced status code be returned for an exchange, yet an operator may refuse a message for several reasons. A client that receives one of these codes should therefore remember that it may not reflect the only reason, or the most important reason, for non-acceptance.

If a server runs several checks and more than one fails, it SHOULD use the code that says multiple methods failed, rather than reporting only the first. One method may always be expected to fail, so naming it tells the sender nothing useful.

The RFC acknowledges that Section 6.1 of RFC 6376 discourages special treatment of messages without a valid DKIM signature, and that some operators ignore this advice. It does not endorse that practice; it only aims to improve interoperability with such operators. One named use case is mailing list software, which processes rejections to remove addresses that are no longer valid. It needs to tell authentication failures apart from a bad recipient address.

Future authentication or policy enforcement technologies should register their own enhanced status codes in the same way.
sections.eli5: A mail server can only give one reason when it says no, even if there were several. So the sender should not assume that reason is the whole story.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
Using these codes reveals local policy about email authentication, which can help someone trying to deliver unwanted mail. There is no obligation to use them. An operator who prefers not to reveal this can keep using a generic code such as 5.7.7, 5.7.1 or even 5.7.0.

The IANA section simply points to Section 3: the codes are added to the Enumerated Status Codes sub-registry of the SMTP Enhanced Status Codes Registry.
sections.eli5: Telling a sender exactly which check failed also tells a bad guy what the rules are. So a server is allowed to keep using vague answers instead.
